column4: Joseph's brothers bring false blood on a shirt, دَمٍ كَذِبٍ; a piece of cloth literally carries a lie in its visible condition, closely matching the section's painted fabric.
The woman who unravels her yarn after spinning it strong turns a textile into the image of oaths used deceitfully; the finished surface and the promised continuation both come apart.
Showy spending, رِئَآءَ ٱلنَّاسِ, is soil spread over rock: rain exposes the stone beneath, exactly as the section's apparent weave is exposed as surface paint.
Bodies that please the eye are likened to propped timber; their upright appearance comes from an external support rather than an inwardly living structure.
أَفَرَءَيْتَ introduces the person who turns away with the same arresting “have you seen?” stance as 107:1; 53:34 then shows what his turning away looks like in action.
He gives a little and then stops, أَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَىٰ, the Quranic enactment of the section's charge, milk, and run that promise continuation but break off.
The hypocrites rise to prayer lazily and only to be seen by people; prayer has its visible posture while its attention remains with the spectators.
The direct question “Why do you say what you do not do?” states the section's claim that lying can be the mismatch between a life's surface and its acts.
This ayah names the saying-doing mismatch as intensely hateful to God, giving the divine judgment beneath the attractive verbal surface described in 61:2.

Righteousness is not the visible turning of faces; care for orphans and the needy, prayer, almsgiving, fidelity, and endurance make people ٱلَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا۟, the actionally truthful opposite of the painted life.
The faithful are humble فِى صَلَاتِهِمْ, inwardly present within their prayer; that exact construction clarifies the section's contrast with being heedless عَن prayer.
Those who remain constant in prayer, دَآئِمُونَ, are the explicit opposite of a prayer-run that stops when the watcher disappears.
Guarding one's prayer supplies the second durable form named in the source section, opposed to possessing only its visible parts.
Prayer and almsgiving are commanded within مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ ٱلدِّينَ; sincere inward orientation makes the visible acts part of the fabric rather than paint on it.
The proposed test makes the shirt's physical state adjudicate two spoken claims: a front tear would make her truthful and him a liar, so cloth can disclose rather than counterfeit truth.
A tear from behind would make her the liar and Joseph truthful; this reverses the section's lying textile by letting a garment's condition expose the speaker.
When the rear tear is actually seen, the surface evidence defeats the fabricated story; visible cloth here reveals what lies underneath the words.
Spending from desire for God's pleasure and inward firmness is a garden that yields under rain; it is the fertile counter-scene to the soil-coated rock of 2:264.
They covenant that if God gives bounty they will donate and become righteous, establishing the beginning whose promise the following ayat test.
Once bounty arrives they withhold it and turn away, so continuation disproves the posture taken at the beginning of their vow.
Their hypocrisy is tied to breaking the promise and lying, بِمَآ أَخْلَفُوا۟ ... وَبِمَا كَانُوا۟ يَكْذِبُونَ; the failed continuation becomes an inward condition.
They say “We believe and obey,” then a group turns away; the second movement exposes the first statement as a surface claim.
When summoned to God's and the Messenger's judgment, a group refuses, showing concretely that the announced obedience in 24:47 never entered conduct.
Hypocrites promise their allies that they will leave with them and help them fight, while God testifies that they are liars; speech launches a movement their acts will not complete.
The promised departure and aid will not occur, and even if they fight they will turn their backs; this is the section's failed charge spelled out as a battlefield prediction.
A mosque is built for harm and division while its builders swear they intended only good; the sacred exterior is paint over a contrary intention, and God calls them liars.
The Prophet is told not to stand in that mosque and is directed to one founded on reverence, distinguishing two outwardly similar structures by their foundation and intent.
A building founded on reverence is set against one on a collapsing bank that falls into fire; what lies beneath the visible building determines whether it stands.
A man's speech about worldly life impresses the listener and he invokes God over his heart, yet the ayah says his hidden reality is fierce hostility.
When he turns away, he destroys crops and offspring; conduct after the impressive speech of 2:204 exposes what its polished surface concealed.
When told to fear God, pride carries him further into sin; the response to correction confirms that the attractive statement in 2:204 was unsupported within.
The hypocrites utter a factually true testimony about the Messenger, yet God calls them liars because their act of witnessing does not correspond to their inner state.
They make their oaths a shield, turning a visible profession into a covering that conceals obstruction.
They believed and then disbelieved, so their hearts were sealed; the sequence is another beginning whose continuation contradicts it.
People say they believe in God and the Last Day while they are not believers, a concise verbal surface over a contrary interior.
When confronted over corruption they call themselves reformers, making their description of their acts contradict the acts themselves.
God identifies them as the actual corrupters, supplying the judgment beneath their self-painted label in 2:11.
They say “We believe” before believers and reverse themselves when alone with their leaders; their profession changes with the watching audience.
The would-be fighters say with their mouths what is not in their hearts; their refusal to follow into battle makes speech, interior, and movement diverge.
Some say “We believe” with their mouths though their hearts have not believed, an exact statement of the section's surface-and-interior split.
The desert Arabs will offer a verbal excuse, saying with their tongues what is not in their hearts; absent conduct and hidden intention qualify the speech.
The desert Arabs are told that faith has not entered their hearts despite their claim “We believe,” sharply separating an outward label from inward reality.
True believers sustain their profession without doubt and expend themselves in action; أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلصَّٰدِقُونَ makes persevering conduct the proof of truth.
People are not left merely to say “We believe”; the claim must pass through a continuing test rather than remain a verbal pattern.
Testing makes the truthful and the liars known, so time and continued action disclose what the initial profession contained.
One says “We believe,” treats human persecution like God's punishment, then claims fellowship when victory comes; affiliation shifts with the visible audience and outcome.
One worships God on an edge, staying for benefit and turning back under trial; conditional worship is precisely a motion that begins but will not carry through.
In the hypocrites' storm-parable they walk whenever lightning gives light and stand still when darkness returns; their movement advances only while conditions please the eye.
Satan adorns the fighters' deeds and promises protection, then turns on his heels when the armies meet; attractive assurance terminates in literal battlefield retreat.
The fighters initially rout the enemy, then lose resolve, dispute, and disobey after seeing what they desire; the assault breaks where the gaze finds its reward.
The question whether people will turn on their heels if the Messenger dies tests whether the professed course continues after its visible leader is gone.
They would follow if gain were near and the journey easy, then swear they could have gone; the unmade journey exposes the oath, and God calls them liars.
Had they truly intended to go out, they would have prepared for it; absent preparation makes inward intention legible through action.
They had already covenanted not to turn their backs, so flight would make a pledged martial beginning fail in its continuation.
Men who صَدَقُوا۟ مَا عَٰهَدُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ عَلَيْهِ fulfill or continue waiting upon their covenant without changing, embodying the section's truthful, unbroken movement.
A pledge to the Messenger is a pledge to God: whoever breaks it harms himself, while fulfillment carries reward; the ayah makes continuation the truth of the initial handclasp.
In the treatment of orphans, God knows the corrupter from the reformer even when both can share a household; the same outward arrangement is judged by conduct and intent.
The condemned person did not believe in the supreme God; 69:34 immediately makes failure toward the poor the visible continuation of that unbelief.
He did not urge feeding the needy, reproducing the surah's move from denied faith to the social act that proves it.
The people of the Fire confess that they were not among those who prayed, beginning a compact reverse portrait of the practices in Surah 107.
They also did not feed the needy, joining failed prayer to failed care as the outward evidence of their condition.
They joined those who treated serious things as play, adding a social performance that carried them away from the acts they named.
They finally confess that they denied the Day of Judgment; the sequence explicitly reads neglect of prayer and food as the lived form of تكذيب بالدين.
He neither affirmed truth nor prayed, but denied and turned away; denial and abandoned prayer are placed in one bodily sequence.
He then goes to his people swaggering, supplying a visible, audience-facing posture after the inward denial and failed prayer of 75:32.
Failure to honor the orphan is presented as the concrete correction to a person's false reading of divine favor and humiliation.
Failure to urge feeding the needy continues the behavioral evidence, closely matching the social proof attached to denial in Surah 107.
The command not to oppress the orphan is the direct behavioral reversal of pushing the orphan away.
The person who gives and is mindful begins the positive sequence whose sustained outcome is measured in the next ayat.
He confirms the best promise, وَصَدَّقَ بِٱلْحُسْنَىٰ, pairing truthful affirmation with the giving action of 92:5.
God eases the giver toward ease, so truthful action opens a course that continues rather than stopping after its first stride.
The contrary person withholds and considers himself self-sufficient; the withheld act supplies the visible side of his denial.
He denies the best promise, وَكَذَّبَ بِٱلْحُسْنَىٰ, explicitly coupling تكذيب with the miserliness of 92:8.
He is eased toward hardship, the terminal course corresponding to the denial and withholding that preceded it.
The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, supplying the enacted care absent from the denier's life.
They say they feed only for God's face and seek no reward or thanks from people, explicitly removing the spectator whose gaze sustains ostentatious action.
أَرَءَيْتَ introduces the man who forbids, echoing 107:1's demand to look at a person whose conduct will disclose him.
What he forbids is a servant praying, bringing prayer itself into the “have you seen?” exposure begun in 96:9.
The question whether that praying servant stands on guidance asks the reader to judge beyond the forbidding man's visible authority.
The servant may command reverence, supplying the action and stance that oppose the denier's coercive display.
The persecutor denies and turns away, كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ, joining the lie to its bodily movement.
“Does he not know that God sees?” relocates the decisive gaze from human spectators to the One who sees the whole act and intent.
Those who spend to be seen by people and do not believe in God or the Last Day make ostentatious giving the visible form of denied judgment.
The fighters leave home boastfully and رِئَآءَ ٱلنَّاسِ; even a public march can orient itself toward watchers rather than its professed end.
Their “prayer” at the House is only whistling and clapping, a visible performance bearing the name of prayer without its inward substance.
The command to fulfill God's covenant and not break confirmed oaths states the durable course that the unraveling-yarn image in 16:92 explains.
Oaths must not become deception lest a firmly planted foot slip; inner fraud turns an apparently settled step into interrupted movement.
God does not take people to account for idle wording in oaths but for what their hearts earn, closely matching the source dictionary sense of holding the swearer to inward intention.
Idle oaths are distinguished from oaths deliberately bound; judgment passes beneath spoken form to the commitment actually made.
Sacrificial flesh and blood do not reach God, while reverence does; the ayah expressly separates visible ritual material from the inward reality that gives it value.
The ayah names camels, asks what the females' wombs contain, and ends by condemning a lie attributed to God; camel, hidden pregnancy, and religious falsehood meet in one scene.
The parallel question about male, female, and what wombs contain demands knowledge “if you are truthful,” preparing the camel version in 6:144 and testing religious claims against concealed fact.
Marked livestock customs are denied divine sanction and called a lie fabricated against God; an animal's visible status has been made to counterfeit religion.
A pregnancy begins as a light burden and later grows heavy and manifest; the womb's developing condition supplies the truthful bodily disclosure named in the source dictionary.
After receiving the sound child for which they prayed, they assign partners regarding the gift; the response fails to continue the intention voiced during pregnancy.
God knows what every female bears and what wombs diminish or increase, placing hidden pregnancy and changing measure within exact knowledge rather than visual inference.
God knew people while they were embryos in their mothers' wombs, so they must not declare themselves pure; unseen origin and inward reverence defeat self-painted virtue before 53:33-34.
Paradise contains rivers of milk whose taste does not change; this is the precise enduring reversal of the source idiom in which expected milk fails and “lies.”
Livestock yield pure, palatable milk from within between waste and blood; what is hidden inside truly provides what the drink's appearance promises.
The same adjective سَاهُونَ describes people immersed in heedlessness, supporting the section's reading of heedlessness as an encompassing distance rather than a small lapse within prayer.
When summoned to go forth, people become heavy and cling to the earth; the command begins a course that their slowed bodies refuse to continue.
A person among the community deliberately lags behind, giving a Quranic bodily scene for the source dictionary's slowing or delaying step.
If success comes, the laggard wishes he had been present for the gain; his movement follows the audience and outcome rather than a stable commitment.
Believers meeting an advancing force are forbidden to turn their backs, directly marking the boundary at which a charge would become the section's failed assault.
Turning away is allowed only for a maneuver or regrouping; the ayah distinguishes purposeful continued combat from simple retreat.
When meeting a force, believers are commanded to stand firm and remember God, the sustained battlefield stance opposed to an attack that stops before its deed is done.
They must not dispute and lose courage, but remain patient; inward cohesion preserves the outward advance begun in 8:45.
The battle instruction continues the blow until the enemy is subdued and bonds are secured, closely matching the source dictionary's assault that does not stop before striking.
God loves fighters in a rank like a solid structure; the compact, mutually supporting formation reverses both the failed charge and the propped timbers whose stance lacks inward support.
The question offers to identify the greatest losers in deeds, directing attention from self-description to what action finally amounts to.
Their effort is lost while they think they are doing beautiful work; the perceived pattern of a life does not match the fabric of its result.
The unbelievers' deeds are a mirage the thirsty person counts as water until arrival reveals nothing and God's account; visible promise, failed continuation, and judgment meet exactly.
An evil deed is made attractive so its doer sees it as good; sight reads an ornamental surface that conduct does not substantiate.
The world's vegetation becomes adorned until its owners think they control it, then is cut down as if it never flourished; an impressive beginning fails its implied promise of duration.
Worldly growth pleases the observer, then dries, yellows, and becomes debris; what delights the eye is tested by whether it remains.
“What is with you runs out, and what is with God remains” states the lasting-versus-failing measure implicit in milk that ceases and an act that stops midway.
The Prophet must not extend his eyes toward the flower of worldly life, a temporary test; the ayah disciplines the gaze and names God's provision as better and more lasting.
The command to establish prayer in one's household and persist patiently in it, وَٱصْطَبِرْ عَلَيْهَا, supplies the durable prayer immediately after the warning against eye-catching display.
A good word is a good tree with a firm root, making truth an inwardly grounded form rather than decoration laid on a surface.
The rooted tree gives fruit repeatedly by its Lord's permission; its continuing yield shows that the promising exterior is supported within.
A bad word is an uprooted tree with no stability, an outward form unable to stand because nothing beneath secures it.
صِبْغَةَ ٱللَّهِ names God's “coloring” and joins it to worship; it offers a transforming coloration of allegiance against the source's dye that merely imitates woven truth.
Literal clothing and adornment are acknowledged, but the garment of reverence is better; the ayah marks the boundary between an attractive surface and the inward clothing that carries value.
The donkey carrying books has the visible burden of revelation without assimilating it, like a patterned exterior unsupported by an inward weave.
Prayer is said to restrain indecency and wrongdoing; its continuing effect in life distinguishes an inwardly operative prayer from a display confined to its postures.
Guarding the prayers and standing devoutly describes attention and preservation, directly opposed to distance from prayer despite performing its pieces.
The believers guard their prayers, repeating within al-Mu'minun the durable opposite of heedlessness from prayer.
Neither trade nor sale distracts these people from remembrance, prayer, and almsgiving; the visible attraction that breaks the gathering in 62:11 cannot stop their course.
The speaker declares prayer, sacrifice, life, and death all for God, placing visible worship inside a single undivided orientation.
Later generations neglect prayer and follow desires; the verse depicts being carried away from prayer as a life-course, rather than a forgotten detail inside one performance.
Those constant in prayer also recognize a fixed share in their wealth, showing prayer continued into material responsibility.
That recognized share belongs to the petitioner and deprived, completing the contrast with prayer accompanied by withholding small aid.
Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminder or injury let the good act retain its promised continuation.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, because a later act can expose and cancel the apparent goodness of the first.
Public charity can be good while concealed charity to the poor is better; the ayah supplies a boundary showing that visibility itself is not hypocrisy, while motive and recipient still matter.
Spending by night and day, secretly and publicly, depicts giving that continues across time and audience instead of stopping when eyes turn away.
The Prophet must not drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening seeking His face; their sustained, inwardly directed worship outweighs social appearance.
He must remain with those who call on their Lord seeking His face and not let his eyes pass beyond them toward worldly adornment; gaze is subordinated to sincere persistence.
Those who order righteousness while forgetting themselves recite the Book yet fail to carry its command into their own action, a direct saying-doing split.
Those who fulfill God's covenant and do not break the pledge model a beginning whose continuation keeps faith with it.
Those who break God's covenant after confirming it show precisely how a solemn beginning can be contradicted by what follows.
Those who say “Our Lord is God” and then remain steadfast make later conduct carry the promise of the initial declaration.
The same sequence of declaring God as Lord and remaining steadfast repeats the section's truthful alternative to a life that starts and stops.
Mistaken naming is excused while what hearts intend is accountable, another explicit judgment beneath outward wording.
Even at resurrection the hypocrites swear to God as they swore to people and imagine it helps them; the final Judge identifies the practiced oath-surface as a lie.
“Rather, you deny the Judgment” names the same object of denial; the following ayat answer it by placing every deed under observation.
Guardians stand over the deniers, relocating the decisive gaze from the human audience to witnesses who do not leave when spectators do.
The watchers are noble recorders, so no visible performance can define itself merely by how people read it.
They know what people do, making deeds rather than surface profession the evidence attached to denial of Judgment in 82:9.
The transgressors are identified as those who deny the Day of Judgment, and 83:14 then identifies what their own earning has done within.
What they earned has rusted over their hearts; repeated deeds become an actual covering on the interior, a dark counterpart to decorative paint on cloth.
The panting chargers stage the animal run developed in the source dictionary; unlike the creature that stops to look behind, their motion is presented as sustained force.
The chargers make a dawn raid, carrying the run of 100:1 into its intended action rather than leaving it an impressive start.
They penetrate the center of the host, completing the charging movement and furnishing a concrete counter-image to the half-finished assault.
The change of prayer-direction distinguishes who follows the Messenger from who turns on his heels; a visible alteration tests whether allegiance continues.
People turn back after guidance has become clear, making later retreat disclose that the earlier advance did not hold.
Those intoxicated may not approach prayer until they know what they are saying; the ayah draws a boundary between bodily performance and conscious presence within it.
Prayer is burdensome except for the inwardly humble, so the same visible act is distinguished by the disposition that inhabits it.
True believers' hearts tremble at God's mention and their faith increases when revelation is recited, locating profession in an inward response that continues to grow.
They establish prayer and spend from their provision, joining worship to material care rather than leaving prayer as a surface pattern.
أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ حَقًّا makes the inward response and acts of 8:2-3 the evidence that belief is real.
The difficult ascent includes feeding on a day of hunger, making costly continued action rather than a displayed gesture the measure.
The recipient is an orphan of near relation, a direct enacted reversal of repelling the orphan.
The same feeding reaches a destitute person in misery, completing the social act rather than withholding small aid.
Only then does the passage say the doer is among the believers who urge endurance and mercy, weaving creed, persistence, and action together.
Tongues falsely label things lawful and unlawful and thereby fabricate a lie against God; religious judgment becomes a verbal surface unsupported by divine warrant.
The earth's adornment is explicitly a test of who is best in deed, so visible beauty is judged by conduct rather than taken as its own truth.
God will make that adorned surface barren ground, exposing the temporary status of the pattern described in 18:7.
Vegetation mingles after rain and then becomes dry fragments scattered by wind; flourishing appearance does not keep its implied promise to remain.
Rain produces crops of varied colors that then wither, yellow, and become debris, repeating the passage from eye-catching surface to exposed impermanence.
A fruitful garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is old and dependent, staging a promising provision whose later failure discloses the need for durable deeds.
Those who establish prayer and spend secretly and publicly hope for a commerce that will never perish; constancy and audience-independent giving answer both the stopped prayer and failed provision.
Those who endure seeking God's face, establish prayer, and spend secretly and publicly embody acts held together by inward aim across changing audiences.
At the Friday call believers must hasten to remembrance and leave trade; this command defines the course that the sight of trade interrupts in 62:11.
After prayer is completed people may disperse and seek God's bounty, showing that commerce has its proper place after worship rather than breaking it midway.
Worship without association is immediately joined to good treatment of orphans and the needy, while proud display is rejected; inner allegiance and social action form one fabric.
The proud are characterized by miserliness, urging others to be miserly, and concealing God's bounty, the social conduct beneath the posture condemned in 4:36.
They take their oaths as a shield and obstruct God's way, a repeated Quranic formulation in which solemn speech becomes a concealing surface for contrary action.
People rejoice in what they have done and love praise for what they did not do; the desired public image is explicitly detached from the deed beneath it.
People who declare themselves pure are corrected by God's prerogative to purify; outward self-description cannot establish the inward state.
The inwardly humble worshippers of the passage are active in almsgiving, carrying prayer into material responsibility toward others.
They faithfully keep trusts and covenants before 23:9 returns to guarded prayer, so the worship is enclosed by durable conduct.
Human beings become withholding when good reaches them; the next ayah's exception makes constancy in prayer answer this concrete refusal to give.
“Except the prayerful” opens the exception to anxious withholding, and 70:23 defines them by continual prayer.
The same people keep trusts and covenants, carrying the durable quality of their prayer into promises and possessions.
They stand by their testimonies, an enacted fidelity of witness immediately before their guarded prayer is restated.
Noah refuses to drive away the believers who will meet their Lord; social appearance cannot justify repelling people whose inward account belongs to God.
“I am not one to drive away the believers” repeats the boundary against judging and repelling the socially weak by their visible status.
The frown is itself a silent bodily statement, beginning a scene in which visible conduct toward a vulnerable seeker is judged.
The triggering event is the blind man's arrival, making the response to one who cannot return the observer's gaze especially pertinent to audience-shaped behavior.
Attention is directed toward the person who considers himself self-sufficient, identifying the socially impressive audience favored by the visible response.
The Prophet gives that self-sufficient person attention, specifying the outward action that the passage corrects.
The other man comes striving, a movement whose inward seriousness contrasts with the privileged audience's self-sufficiency.
He comes in reverent fear, supplying the hidden quality beneath the unimpressive exterior.
Attention is diverted from the striving, reverent man; the gaze and social audience visibly redirect the encounter.
A secure town with abundant provision denies God's favors and is made to taste the garment of hunger and fear because of its deeds; outward plenty becomes a garment matching inner conduct.
A messenger came with clear signs, but the town denied him and punishment seized it, identifying the تكذيب beneath the changed garment of 16:112.
Livestock provide drink from what is in their bellies and many other benefits; the Quranic animal genuinely supplies from within what its condition offers outwardly.
Only God knows what is in the wombs and what a person will earn tomorrow, marking the limit of reading hidden truth or future continuation from visible signs.
No fruit leaves its sheath and no female conceives or gives birth outside God's knowledge; enclosed fruit and womb alike place hidden content under exact knowledge.
At Hunayn impressive numbers avail nothing and the fighters turn away fleeing; visible strength fails at the moment the charge should continue.
Some claim their houses are exposed although they are not and seek leave only to flee; a verbal pretext covers the intended retreat.
God knows the hinderers who summon their fellows away and come to battle only a little, making interrupted martial movement evidence of their stance.
Their eyes roll in fear during danger, then their tongues become sharp when danger passes; bodily gaze and speech change with the watching circumstance, and the ayah denies their faith.
Those who ask for a surah reveal a death-struck gaze when decisive fighting is prescribed; the requested beginning falters when action arrives.
Obedience and a fitting word are named, then the ayah says truthfulness to God would be better once the matter is resolved; continuation tests the spoken posture.
Moses commands his people to enter the holy land and not turn on their backs, a direct movement boundary for the source dictionary's advance that either holds or fails.
Invented rules mark crops and livestock as restricted and even suppress God's name over animals; visible animal categories are made to carry a fabricated religious claim.
They make what is inside livestock bellies lawful for men and forbidden to wives, with another rule if it is stillborn; hidden animal contents become material for false religious distinctions.
Those who prohibit God's provision through invention are declared lost and unguided, giving the judgment on the animal-and-womb fabrications in 6:138-139.
People turn God's provision into “lawful” and “unlawful”; the question asks whether God permitted it or they fabricate a lie against Him.
The disbelievers' deeds are ashes scattered by a violent wind, so an apparent accumulation proves unable to endure or deliver what it seemed to promise.
When invited to seek forgiveness, the hypocrites turn their heads and are seen withdrawing arrogantly; their bodies disclose the stance concealed by polished appearance.
They instruct others not to spend on those around the Messenger until they disperse, making withholding the social action beneath their professed affiliation.
Wealth and children must not distract believers from remembrance; the ayah names the visible attractions that can pull worship off its course.
One who hopes to meet the Lord must do righteous work and associate no one in worship, joining outward deed to an undivided addressee rather than a human audience.
The command to worship God while making the religion sincere for Him places visible worship wholly inside its intended allegiance.
Pure religion belongs to God, while claimed intermediaries are justified by a stated intention; God judges the dispute and does not guide the liar, testing the explanation beneath worship's surface.
In danger at sea people call on God with sincere religion and promise gratitude if rescued, establishing an inward profession whose continuation will immediately be tested.
Once rescued they transgress on earth, so the safe continuation contradicts the sincere crisis-prayer and promise of 10:22.
Ship passengers call on God with sincere religion, then associate partners once brought ashore; one ayah contains both the inward-sounding beginning and its failed continuation.
Joseph's brothers report that they went racing and that a wolf ate him, adding that Jacob would not believe them though they were “truthful”; the rehearsed speech precedes the lying shirt in 12:18.
People are commanded to act because God, the Messenger, and believers will see their deeds, and God will disclose them; the decisive gaze remains when the performer's chosen audience does not.
Believers are warned not to become like earlier communities whose hearts hardened as time lengthened; duration reveals whether an initial reception remains alive within.
They swear their strongest oaths that they would go out if commanded, but are told not to swear and that known obedience is required; deeds, not emphatic surface speech, are the test.
Hatred has already appeared from opponents' mouths while what their breasts conceal is greater, distinguishing the visible leakage from the deeper interior.
They say “We believe” when they meet believers but bite their fingertips in rage when alone, changing their visible posture with the audience.
Those with diseased hearts are asked whether they think God will not expose their resentments, directly announcing that the concealed layer cannot remain hidden.
They could be recognized by visible marks and are already recognizable by the tone of speech, while God knows deeds; body, voice, and action disclose what lies within.
